Supporting Information
Metabolic interactions enable aerobic degradation of the environmental pollutant BDE-47
Running title: Synergistic aerobic degradation of BDE-47

Piaopiao Pan, Ning-Yi Zhou*

State Key Laboratory of Microbial Metabolism, Joint International Research Laboratory of Metabolic and Developmental Sciences, and School of Life Sciences and Biotechnology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 200240 Shanghai, China

*Correspondence to Ning-Yi Zhou, Email: ningyi.zhou@sjtu.edu.cn



Number of Pages: 24
Number of Figures: 16
Number of Tables: 9 (Tables 6-9 in the file titled "Supplemental Tables 6-9")


Supplemental Figures:

Figure S1. LC-MS analysis of BDE-47 transformation intermediate by strain YL-JM2C. The left panel shows the extracted ion chromatogram peaks of the 2,4-DBP standard and the product captured during whole-cell biotransformation, while the right panel presents their corresponding mass spectra.


Figure S2. Whole-cell biotransformation of BDE-47 by triclosan-induced and uninduced (glucose-pretreated) cells of strain YL-JM2C. The residual BDE-47 concentration was determined at different time points using HPLC. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (n = 3).


Figure S3. Transformation of BDE-47 by E. coli cells expressing dioxygenase TcsAaAb. (A) Proposed mechanism for the TcsAaAb-mediated transformation of BDE-47. The compound in the bracket was not detected. (B-C) Identification of BDE-47 transformation products through GC-MS. Extracted ion chromatogram peaks and mass spectra for 3,5-DBC (B) and 2,4-DBP (C) are shown.


Figure S4. Functional characterization of purified TcsC. (A) Reaction scheme of 3,5-DBC biotransformation by TcsC. (B) SDS-PAGE analysis of TcsC expression and purification. Lane M, protein marker; lane 1, cell extract of E. coli BL21(DE3) harboring pET-tcsC; lane 2, protein flow-through fluid; lanes 3-6, elution buffer containing 250 mM imidazole. The arrow indicates purified TcsC. (C) Spectra of reaction mixtures containing Tris-HCl buffer and 3,5-DBC (negative control). (D) Spectra of reaction mixtures containing Tris-HCl buffer, 3,5-DBC and purified TcsC. (E) Extracted ion chromatogram peak corresponding to the ring-cleavage product generated by TcsC. (F) Mass spectrum of the ring-cleavage product.


Figure S5. Functional characterization of the downstream enzymes TcsD, TcsE, and TcsF involved in the conversion of 2,4-dibromomuconate to 3-oxoadipate. Reactions were performed using crude cell extracts prepared from E. coli expressing the respective enzymes. Schematic representation of the reactions catalyzed by TcsD, TcsE, and TcsF is shown at the top. (A-C) UV-visible spectral changes during the conversion of 2,4-dibromomuconate to 2-bromodienelactone (A), 2-bromodienelactone to 2-bromomaleylacetate (B), and 2-bromomaleylacetate to 3-oxoadipate (C). (D-F) Extracted ion chromatogram peaks of the reaction products. (G-I) Corresponding mass spectra confirming the identities of 2-bromodienelactone, 2-bromomaleylacetate, and 3-oxoadipate.


Figure S6. Functional characterization of PcaIJ and PcaF from R. wittichii YL-JM2C involved in the 3-oxoadipate pathway. (A) Proposed reactions catalyzed by PcaIJ and PcaF for the conversion of 3-oxoadipate into central carbon metabolism intermediates. (B) UV spectrum scanning of 3-oxoadipate transformation catalyzed by cell extract of recombinant E. coli expressing PcaIJ. The arrow indicates the formation of 3-oxoadipyl-CoA-Mg2+ complex (305 nm). (C) UV spectrum scanning of 3-oxoadipyl-CoA cleavage catalyzed by cell extract of recombinant E. coli expressing PcaF. The arrow indicates the disappearance of 3-oxoadipyl-CoA-Mg2+ complex.


Figure S7. The tfd gene cluster and 2,4-D degradation pathway in Cupriavidus necator JMP134. The five ORFs were organized and assigned as follows: tfdD II C II E II F II and tfdB II (in short, the tfd II cluster), by analogy to tfdCDEF and tfdB (the tfd I cluster). Primer extension analysis of mRNA isolated from 2,4-D-grown R. eutropha JMP134 identified a single transcription start site in front of the first gene of the cluster, tfdD II , suggesting an operon-like organization for the tfd II genes. By expressing each ORF in Escherichia coli , we confirmed that tfdD II coded for a chloromuconate cycloisomerase, tfdC II coded for a chlorocatechol 1,2-dioxygenase, tfdE II coded for a dienelactone hydrolase, tfdF II coded for a maleylacetate reductase, and tfdB II coded for a chlorophenol hydroxylase. Dot blot hybridizations of mRNA isolated from R. eutropha JMP134 showed that both tfd I and tfd II genes are transcribed upon induction with 2,4-D. Thus, the functions encoded by the tfd II genes seem to be redundant with respect to those of the tfd I cluster. Figure S10. Growth curve of strain JMP134 on 2,4-dibromophenol (2,4-DBP). Strain JMP134 was cultivated in MSM supplemented with 100 mM 2,4-DBP as the sole carbon source, and growth was monitored by measuring OD600 over time. A substrate-free culture served as the negative control.


Figure S11. Comparison of BDE-47 degradation efficiency between the transwell and mixed groups over time. Two-tailed Student's t tests were performed for statistical analysis. ns indicates no significant difference (P ≥ 0.05) between the two groups at the corresponding time point. No accumulation of 2,4-DBP was detected in either group throughout the incubation process. The transwell assays were performed in a 24-well transwell plate (0.4 μm pore size; Jet Biofil). For transwell group, 100 mL of strain JMP134 suspension (OD₆₀₀ = 0.25) was added to the upper insert, and the lower chamber with 100 mL of strain YL-JM2C suspension (OD₆₀₀ = 0.25) plus 300 mL of MSM, supplemented with BDE-47 to a final concentration of 20 µM. For the Mixed group (without physical separation), the same amounts of JMP134 and YL-JM2C suspensions (100 mL each, OD₆₀₀ = 0.25) were co-inoculated directly into a single well of a 24-well plate containing 300 mL of MSM supplemented with 20 µM BDE-47.


Figure S12. Dynamics of the two bacterial strains during BDE-47 degradation. The BDE-47 concentration is shown as line, and bacterial abundance is shown as histogram by cell densities (cells/mL). Blue bars represent strain YL-JM2C, and pink bars represent strain JMP134. Both strains were inoculated at 5% (v/v) from culture with an OD600 of 1.0 into MSM supplemented with 50 μM BDE-47, and replenished with another 50 μM BDE-47 on day 5 and 10. Bacterial abundances were determined by qPCR targeting a strain-specific region of the 16S rRNA gene after normalization against the 16S rRNA gene copy numbers per genome (six copies for strain JMP134 and two copies for strain YL-JM2C).

Figure S13. Effects of temperature (A) and pH (B) on BDE-47 degradation by the synthetic consortium. The BDE-47 degradation percentage was determined after a 12-h incubation. The initial concentration of BDE-47 was 50 μM, with the bacterial culture inoculated at an OD600 of 4.0.


Figure S14. Conserved domain analysis and phylogenetic analysis of TcsAa homologs retrieved from NR database at 35% identity threshold. (A) Multiple sequence alignment of TcsAa and retrieved homologs. Residues labeled with position numbers are involved in Rieske-type [2Fe–2S] cluster binding and mononuclear Fe²⁺ coordination. Residue positions are numbered according to the TcsAa sequence. (B) Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis of TcsAa homologs and functionally characterized Rieske dioxygenases.

Figure S15. Phylogenetic tree of TfdB homologous proteins. The sequences were retrieved via BLASTP against NR database with an identity threshold of 50%. Proteins TfdBI and TfdBII are marked with green circles, and RwTfdB is marked with a red circle. The branch highlighted in orange represents the clade containing TfdBI and TfdBII, and the protein sequences within this clade are proposed to be potential candidates possessing activity towards 2,4-DBP.


Figure S16. BDE-47 degradation and bromide ion release by the synthetic consortium. Both strains were adjusted to an OD600 of 1.0 and inoculated at 5% (v/v, each). Control experiments were prepared with autoclaved cell suspensions under same conditions. (A) BDE-47 degradation by the synthetic consortium in MSM supplemented with 0.4 μM BDE-47. (B) Bromide ion release corresponding to the degradation experiment shown in (A). Bromide ion concentrations were quantified by ion chromatography at 0 h and 12 h. Organohalide-respiring bacteria (OHRB) can attenuate PBDEs via reductive debromination, but often producing toxic end-products. Debromination of PBDEs to diphenyl ether remains a rare phenomenon and is so far specifically associated with Dehalococcoides isolated from e-waste polluted sites. The occurrence of PBDE debromination in other ecosystems and underpinning OHRB are underexplored. Here we found that debromination of PBDEs is a common trait of sewage sludge microbiota, and diphenyl ether was produced as the end-product at varying quantities (0.6–52.9% mol of the parent PBDEs) in 76 of 84 cultures established with bioreactor sludge. Diverse debromination pathways converting PBDEs to diphenyl ether, including several new routes, were identified. Although Dehalococcoides contributed to PBDE debromination, Dehalogenimonas, Dehalobacter, and uncultivated Dehalococcoidia likely played more important roles than previously recognized. Multiple reductive dehalogenase genes (including bdeA, pcbA4, pteA, and tceA) were also prevalent and coexisted in bioreactor sludge. Collectively, these findings contribute to enhancing our comprehension of the environmental fate of PBDEs, expanding the diversity of microorganisms catalyzing PBDE debromination, and developing consortia for bioremediation application.","container-title":"Environmental Science &amp; Technology","DOI":"10.1021/acs.est.4c00906","ISSN":"0013-936X","issue":"30","journalAbbreviation":"Environ. Sphingomonas sp, strain YL-JM2C, isolated from activated sludge of a wastewater treatment plant, was very effective on degrading TCS. Response surface methodology (RSM) was applied to optimize the conditions like temperature and pH. From RSM, the optimal TCS degradation conditions were found to be 30 °C and pH 7.0. Under optimal conditions, strain YL-JM2C completely mineralized TCS (5 mg L(-1)) within 72 h. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis revealed that 2,4-dichlorophenol, 2-chlorohydroquinone and hydroquinone are three main by-products of TCS. Furthermore, stable isotope experimental results revealed that the (13)C12-TCS was completely mineralized into CO2 and part of heavier carbon ((13)C) of labeled TCS was utilized by strain YL-JM2C to synthesize fatty acids (PLFAs). Cell surface hydrophobicity (CSH) and degradation test results suggested that the strain could enhance degradation capacity of TCS through increasing CSH. In addition, the bacterium also completely degraded spiked TCS (5 mg L(-1)) in wastewater collected from the wastewater treatment plant. Hence, these results suggest that the strain has potential to remediate TCS in the environment.","container-title":"Scientific Reports","DOI":"10.1038/srep21965","ISSN":"2045-2322","journalAbbreviation":"Sci.  ADDIN ZOTERO_ITEM CSL_CITATION {"citationID":"xAacIWhj","properties":{"unsorted":false,"formattedCitation":"[5]","plainCitation":"[5]","noteIndex":0},"citationItems":[{"id":23805,"uris":["http://zotero.org/users/9631149/items/PJU7R8S7"],"itemData":{"id":23805,"type":"article-journal","abstract":"Background: Cupriavidus necator JMP134 is a Gram-negative b-proteobacterium able to grow on a variety of aromatic and chloroaromatic compounds as its sole carbon and energy source.\nMethodology/Principal Findings: Its genome consists of four replicons (two chromosomes and two plasmids) containing a total of 6631 protein coding genes. Comparative analysis identified 1910 core genes common to the four genomes compared (C. necator JMP134, C. necator H16, C. metallidurans CH34, R. solanacearum GMI1000). Although secondary chromosomes found in the Cupriavidus, Ralstonia, and Burkholderia lineages are all derived from plasmids, analyses of the plasmid partition proteins located on those chromosomes indicate that different plasmids gave rise to the secondary chromosomes in each lineage. The C. necator JMP134 genome contains 300 genes putatively involved in the catabolism of aromatic compounds and encodes most of the central ring-cleavage pathways. This strain also shows additional metabolic capabilities towards alicyclic compounds and the potential for catabolism of almost all proteinogenic amino acids. This remarkable catabolic potential seems to be sustained by a high degree of genetic redundancy, most probably enabling this catabolically versatile bacterium with different levels of metabolic responses and alternative regulation necessary to cope with a challenging environment. From the comparison of Cupriavidus genomes, it is possible to state that a broad metabolic capability is a general trait for Cupriavidus genus, however certain specialization towards a nutritional niche (xenobiotics degradation, chemolithoautotrophy or symbiotic nitrogen fixation) seems to be shaped mostly by the acquisition of ‘‘specialized’’ plasmids.\nConclusions/Significance: The availability of the complete genome sequence for C. necator JMP134 provides the groundwork for further elucidation of the mechanisms and regulation of chloroaromatic compound biodegradation.","container-title":"PLoS ONE","DOI":"10.1371/journal.pone.0009729","ISSN":"1932-6203","issue":"3","journalAbbreviation":"PLOS One","language":"en","page":"e9729","source":"DOI.org (Crossref)","title":"The complete multipartite genome sequence of &lt;i&gt;Cupriavidus necator&lt;/i&gt; JMP134, a versatile pollutant degrader","volume":"5","author":[{"family":"Lykidis","given":"Athanasios"},{"family":"Pérez-Pantoja","given":"Danilo"},{"family":"Ledger","given":"Thomas"},{"family":"Mavromatis","given":"Kostantinos"},{"family":"Anderson","given":"Iain J."},{"family":"Ivanova","given":"Natalia N."},{"family":"Hooper","given":"Sean D."},{"family":"Lapidus","given":"Alla"},{"family":"Lucas","given":"Susan"},{"family":"González","given":"Bernardo"},{"family":"Kyrpides","given":"Nikos C."}],"editor":[{"family":"Ahmed","given":"Niyaz"}],"issued":{"date-parts":[["2010",3,22]]}}}],"schema":"https://github.com/citation-style-language/schema/raw/master/csl-citation.json"} [5]

A set of conditions is described under which about one in every 400 plasmid molecules produces a transformed cell. These conditions include cell growth in medium containing elevated levels of Mg2+, and incubation of the cells at 0 degrees C in a solution of Mn2+, Ca2+, Rb+ or K+, dimethyl sulfoxide, dithiothreitol, and hexamine cobalt (III). Transformation efficiency declines linearly with increasing plasmid size. Relaxed and supercoiled plasmids transform with similar probabilities. Non-transforming DNAs compete consistent with mass. No significant variation is observed between competing DNAs of different source, complexity, length or form. Competition with both transforming and non-transforming plasmids indicates that each cell is capable of taking up many DNA molecules, and that the establishment of a transformation event is neither helped nor hindered significantly by the presence of multiple plasmids.","container-title":"Journal of Molecular Biology","DOI":"10.1016/s0022-2836(83)80284-8","ISSN":"0022-2836","issue":"4","journalAbbreviation":"J.  ADDIN ZOTERO_ITEM CSL_CITATION {"citationID":"Dqe3tvb6","properties":{"unsorted":false,"formattedCitation":"[7]","plainCitation":"[7]","noteIndex":0},"citationItems":[{"id":29602,"uris":["http://zotero.org/users/9631149/items/EM9YRQKG"],"itemData":{"id":29602,"type":"article-journal","abstract":"A gene expression system based on bacteriophage T7 RNA polymerase has been developed. T7 RNA polymerase is highly selective for its own promoters, which do not occur naturally in Escherichia coli. A relatively small amount of T7 RNA polymerase provided from a cloned copy of T7 gene 1 is sufficient to direct high-level transcription from a T7 promoter in a multicopy plasmid. Such transcription can proceed several times around the plasmid without terminating, and can be so active that transcription by E. coli RNA polymerase is greatly decreased. When a cleavage site for RNase III is introduced, discrete RNAs of plasmid length can accumulate. The natural transcription terminator from T7 DNA also works effectively in the plasmid. Both the rate of synthesis and the accumulation of RNA directed by T7 RNA polymerase can reach levels comparable with those for ribosomal RNAs in a normal cell. These high levels of accumulation suggest that the RNAs are relatively stable, perhaps in part because their great length and/or stem-and-loop structures at their 3' ends help to protect them against exonucleolytic degradation. It seems likely that a specific mRNA produced by T7 RNA polymerase can rapidly saturate the translational machinery of E. coli, so that the rate of protein synthesis from such an mRNA will depend primarily on the efficiency of its translation. When the mRNA is efficiently translated, a target protein can accumulate to greater than 50% of the total cell protein in three hours or less. We have used two ways to deliver active T7 RNA polymerase to the cell; infection by a lambda derivative that carries gene 1, or induction of a chromosomal copy of gene 1 under control of the lacUV5 promoter. When gene 1 is delivered by infection, very toxic target genes can be maintained silent in the cell until T7 RNA polymerase is introduced, when they rapidly become expressed at high levels. When gene 1 is resident in the chromosome, even the very low basal levels of T7 RNA polymerase present in the uninduced cell can prevent the establishment of plasmids carrying toxic target genes, or make the plasmid unstable.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 400 WORDS)","container-title":"Journal of Molecular Biology","DOI":"10.1016/0022-2836(86)90385-2","ISSN":"0022-2836","issue":"1","journalAbbreviation":"J.
